title: CopyFrom bulk loads, batches, context timeouts and cancellation
summary: CopyFrom streams rows over the COPY protocol and loads 100k rows in one all-or-nothing statement; a Batch sends many statements in one round trip. Give every query a deadline, and choose whether it is enforced by closing the connection, by a cancel request, or by the server's statement_timeout.

examples.title: 100,000 rows with CopyFrom, and a load that fails as a whole

annotations.note: CopyFrom runs COPY ... FROM STDIN in binary format: one statement, rows streamed without a round trip each. pgx's own docs say it can beat INSERT with as few as 5 rows. The program prints no timing because it varies; the run panel's duration covers the whole program, connect and summary query included.
CopyFromSlice asks for one row at a time, so nothing holds 100k []any at once. CopyFromFunc does the same for sources without a length, such as a csv.Reader; CopyFromRows wraps a ready [][]any.

A single bad row fails the whole COPY and loads nothing: the row 100001 before the duplicate is gone too. The aborted rows still take disk space until VACUUM. COPY's ON_ERROR ignore doesn't help here: it only applies to text and csv input, and pgx sends binary.
Under this database's C.UTF-8 locale, ORDER BY city puts İstanbul and İzmir after Muğla, because İ (U+0130) sorts by code point. The ICU collation tr-x-icu gives the order a Turkish reader expects.

examples.title: A Batch is one round trip and one implicit transaction

annotations.note: Queue only records the statement; nothing is sent yet. The callback sees each result in order. Capturing name is safe because since Go 1.22 every loop iteration has its own variable.
SendBatch sends everything at once, and Close reads every result and runs the callbacks. Close must happen before the connection is used again, and its error is the batch's error.
Without an explicit BEGIN, the batch runs as one implicit transaction: the duplicate rolls back the "sql" insert queued before it, and the DELETE after it never executes, so its callback never runs.
The table shows only batch 1's rows. array_agg needs its own ORDER BY for a deterministic order, and pgx scans the text[] straight into a []string.

examples.title: Three ways a slow query ends, and what each leaves behind

annotations.note: The default: when the context expires, pgx sends PostgreSQL a cancel request and closes the connection. The error wraps context.DeadlineExceeded; a pool simply discards the dead connection, a lone *pgx.Conn must reconnect.

CancelRequestContextWatcherHandler asks the server to cancel and waits for its answer, so the connection survives. The error is then the server's 57014, not DeadlineExceeded: check ctx.Err() to know a deadline caused it. DeadlineDelay caps how long it waits.

statement_timeout is enforced by the server alone, with no client context involved; RuntimeParams makes it the session default on every connection (on a pool: cfg.ConnConfig.RuntimeParams). The connection stays healthy.
Call cancel as soon as the work is done, not only on error: a context with a timer holds resources until it fires or is cancelled.

use_cases: CopyFrom: imports, seeding test data, nightly loads from another system, copying between databases
Batch: many small independent statements per request (several inserts, a read after a write) without paying a round trip each
Context deadlines: every query in a request handler, bounded by the request's own deadline
statement_timeout: a server-side ceiling for a role or service, so one bad query can't run for hours
strengths: COPY is PostgreSQL's fastest way in, and pgx exposes it with Go values; database/sql has no equivalent without Raw
A batch removes round trips without string-building a multi-row INSERT, and each statement keeps its own parameters
Cancellation is a context, the same mechanism as for HTTP calls, so a client disconnect can stop the query it started
Unlike JDBC's setQueryTimeout (whole seconds, set per statement), one context carries a single deadline through every call of a request, HTTP and SQL alike
weaknesses: COPY is all or nothing and stops at the first bad row; reporting which rows were bad needs validation first or a staging table
CopyFrom needs binary encodings for every column: enum and other custom types must be registered with the connection first
The default cancellation closes the connection, which costs a reconnect; the polite handler opens an extra connection to deliver the cancel request, which PostgreSQL's protocol makes inherently racy

pitfalls.title: Queries without a deadline
pitfalls.detail: context.Background() in a handler lets a slow query outlive the request. Use the request's context (r.Context()) and, for long work, context.WithTimeout on top of it.

pitfalls.title: Using the connection before closing the batch
pitfalls.detail: BatchResults must be closed before the connection runs anything else; until then the connection is busy reading the batch's results.

pitfalls.title: Creating a table and using it in the same batch
pitfalls.detail: With the default exec mode pgx may prepare every queued statement before running any of them, so a statement that refers to a table created earlier in the batch can fail. Run DDL first, then the batch.

pitfalls.title: Building one giant INSERT string
pitfalls.detail: Concatenating VALUES (...) rows risks injection and runs into the 65535 bind-parameter limit if you parameterize it. CopyFrom has neither problem.

quiz.q: The 60,000th row of a 100,000-row CopyFrom violates a CHECK constraint. How many rows are in the table afterwards?
quiz.why: COPY is one statement: an error aborts it, and the rows it had already written stay invisible until VACUUM removes them.

quiz.q: A batch queues INSERT a, INSERT b (which fails), INSERT c, with no BEGIN. What is committed?
quiz.why: SendBatch runs the queued statements in one implicit transaction unless the batch contains its own transaction control.

quiz.q: With pgx's default settings, a query's context deadline expires. What happens to the connection?
options: pgx sends a cancel request and closes it
quiz.why: The default handler interrupts the network read and closes the connection, after asking the server to cancel the query.

quiz.q: You want slow queries stopped but connections kept. Which options do that?
quiz.why: Both make the server cancel the statement (57014) and leave the connection usable; a context deadline with the default handler closes it.

PostgreSQL: statement_timeout and other client settings

body:
## Concept

Three tools for doing a lot, or for giving up on time.

**CopyFrom** uses PostgreSQL's COPY protocol: one `COPY ... FROM STDIN` statement, then
the rows streamed in binary. No per-row round trip, no per-row statement. You hand it a
`CopyFromSource`: `CopyFromRows` for a `[][]any`, `CopyFromSlice(n, fn)` to produce row
`i` on demand, `CopyFromFunc` for a stream of unknown length. Being one statement, it is
all or nothing.

**Batch** queues ordinary statements, each with its own parameters, and `SendBatch` sends
them together. Results come back in order, to callbacks or to `BatchResults`. Without its
own `BEGIN`, the batch runs as one implicit transaction.

**Cancellation** is a context. Every pgx call takes one; when it expires, what happens
depends on the connection's context-watcher handler: by default pgx asks the server to
cancel and closes the connection; `CancelRequestContextWatcherHandler` asks and keeps it.
Independently, the server's `statement_timeout` cancels any statement running longer than
the limit, and the connection stays usable either way.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: CopyFrom is the PgJDBC `CopyManager` with typed values instead of CSV text; a
  Batch is closer to pipelining than to `addBatch`, because each statement can return rows.
  A context replaces `Statement.setQueryTimeout` and `cancel()` with one mechanism.
- Python: psycopg 3's `cursor.copy()` and `executemany` are the equivalents; asyncio's
  `wait_for` around a query plays the context's role.
- Node: `pg-copy-streams` adds COPY to node-postgres; an `AbortSignal` passed down the call
  chain is the closest thing to a context.
- C: libpq's `PQputCopyData` and pipeline mode are the same protocol features, which pgx
  implements natively rather than wrapping libpq; `PQcancel` is the cancel request.

## Design notes

Put deadlines where the work starts: an HTTP handler passes `r.Context()` down, so a
client that disconnects cancels its queries; background jobs set `context.WithTimeout`.
Add `statement_timeout` as a server-side backstop for the whole service, set on the
pool's `ConnConfig.RuntimeParams` or with `ALTER ROLE ... SET statement_timeout`, so a
forgotten context can't run a query for hours. `SET LOCAL statement_timeout` inside a
transaction raises or lowers it for one unit of work.

For imports, validate in Go before CopyFrom, or COPY into a staging table without
constraints and move the good rows with one `INSERT ... SELECT`; the
`sql.files-movement` module shows the staging pattern. Measure with your own data and
indexes: every index on the target table is maintained row by row during the load, which
is why PostgreSQL's bulk-loading advice suggests creating indexes after a large initial
load.
